timeline.title: UNESCO backs the idea before it exists
timeline.text: UNESCO's General Conference commends the planned township, the first of five non-binding resolutions of support (1966, 1968, 1970, 1983, 2017) that gave Auroville international standing.

timeline.title: Inauguration and the four-point Charter
timeline.text: On 28 Feb 1968 some 5,000 people gathered as youths from 124 nations and all Indian states put soil in an urn. The Mother's Charter says Auroville belongs "to nobody in particular".

timeline.title: Pioneers start greening an eroded plateau
timeline.text: Early settlers found baked red earth cut by monsoon gullies. From the early 1970s they built bunds and check dams and planted trees on a massive scale, slowly rebuilding soil and forest.

timeline.title: Matrimandir foundation stone laid
timeline.text: Work on the Matrimandir, the gold-clad 'soul of the city', began on 21 Feb 1971. Its inner chamber opened in 1994 and the structure was completed in 2008, 37 years later.

timeline.title: Founder dies; split with the Society
timeline.text: After The Mother died in 1973, serious rifts grew between residents and the Sri Aurobindo Society, which legally held Auroville's assets and managed its affairs.

timeline.title: Government takes over management
timeline.text: Parliament passed the Auroville (Emergency Provisions) Act 1980, putting the township's management under the central government, meant as a temporary measure.

timeline.title: Supreme Court upholds the takeover
timeline.text: In S.P. Mittal v. Union of India (8 Nov 1982) a five-judge bench upheld the 1980 Act, holding that neither the Society nor Auroville was a religious denomination under Articles 25-26.

timeline.title: Auroville Foundation Act creates 3-part rule
timeline.text: The Act vested all of Auroville's assets in a statutory Foundation with three bodies: a centrally nominated Governing Board, an International Advisory Council and a Residents' Assembly.

timeline.title: Master Plan for 50,000 approved
timeline.text: The Universal Township Master Plan (Perspective 2025), drafted with residents from 1999 on the 'Galaxy' concept, was approved by the education (HRD) ministry in 2001 and gazetted in 2010.

timeline.title: 'Acres for Auroville' land drive launched
timeline.text: A global campaign began on 15 Aug 2014 to buy missing plots. Auroville says it has secured about half its land; ~10% of the City Area and ~65% of the Green Belt are still unbought.

timeline.title: New Secretary and Governing Board
timeline.text: IAS officer Jayanti S. Ravi became Foundation Secretary from 5 Jul 2021; in Oct 2021 a new Governing Board was named, chaired by Tamil Nadu Governor R.N. Ravi.

timeline.title: Crown road clearing hits the Youth Centre
timeline.text: In December 2021 crews cleared a path for the Crown ring road, partly demolishing the Youth Centre; residents say 900+ trees were felled within days. Protests followed and the NGT stayed further felling.

timeline.title: Green Tribunal conditions development
timeline.text: In April 2022 the NGT let the Crown Road be finished in tree-free stretches, barred other construction until environmental clearance, and ordered a township plan and 1:10 replanting.

timeline.title: Supreme Court overturns NGT limits
timeline.text: On 17 Mar 2025, after a Dec 2023 interim stay, the Supreme Court set aside the NGT order as outside its jurisdiction, saying the right to development 'equally claims priority'.

timeline.title: Court: Residents' Assembly is advisory
timeline.text: Same day, the Court held residents have no right to sit on councils formed by the Governing Board and that the Residents' Assembly's functions are confined to advising the Board.

timeline.title: Parliament panel urges 5-year visas
timeline.text: Parliament's education committee (371st report, Dec 2025) urged five-year visas as the norm for residents and less outside interference, and floated 'Institution of National Importance' status.

timeline.title: Visa fears among foreign residents
timeline.text: Accounts gathered by AFP describe dozens of visa refusals and four expulsions. Secretary Ravi says 99% of applicants get visas and those refused broke the law or obstructed government work.

timeline.title: Census: 3,527 residents, 60 nations
timeline.text: Auroville's 2026 census counts 3,527 residents (2,865 adults, 662 children) from 60 nationalities, 1,888 of them Indian: about 7% of the 50,000 the plan foresees.

lessons.lesson: Auroville began with its assets held by a sponsoring society; after the founder died, a society-resident split ended in a 1980 state takeover. Create a durable legal entity that residents control, with clear asset ownership, from day one.

After 58 years Auroville holds only about half its master-plan land (about 65% of the Green Belt is still missing) as prices and speculation rose around it. Buy a contiguous core early, in a country whose land law lets your entity own it.

Auroville's land and buildings were paid for largely by donations, much of it from abroad. Today all foreign donations must go through the government-run Auroville Foundation. Check foreign-contribution rules (India: FCRA) and who controls the receiving body.

Foreigners can only settle on an Entry visa backed by a letter from the Foundation's government-appointed Secretary; tourist visas can't be converted. Residents report withheld letters, which officials deny. Prefer rights-based residency routes.

The 1988 Act gave residents an Assembly but put power in a centrally nominated Board and Secretary, and in 2025 the Supreme Court held the Assembly is advisory. A special law can protect a project and also subordinate it to whoever governs.

The Crown road dispute ran through the Green Tribunal, Madras High Court and Supreme Court from 2021 to 2025, with stays and reversals. Courts gave both sides a hearing, but litigation was slow, costly and unpredictable. Weigh judicial independence and speed.

Auroville's statute barely changed, yet residents and press describe a sharp change of direction after new central appointments in 2021. Projects that depend on official goodwill need protections that survive changes of government.

Almost all of Auroville's water is groundwater. Over-pumping from thousands of regional borewells is lowering the water table and raising seawater-intrusion risk. Bunds and check dams helped, but one community can't fix a watershed. Check aquifers first.

Pioneers settled a gullied, eroded plateau, and bunding plus mass tree planting rebuilt soil, forest and wildlife. Degraded land is cheaper and can be restored, but plan for decades of work before it can feed a town.

Auroville's plots are interspersed with Tamil villages, and thousands of villagers work there daily. Land deals, jobs and inequality shape the relationship. Build shared benefits and fair, transparent land dealings with neighbours from the start.

Being 10 km from Puducherry brings visitors, volunteers and markets, but also sprawl, speculation and what Auroville calls 'often unregulated' development at its edges. Near-city sites need zoning protection or a buffer you own.

Auroville's coast gets extreme weather: a 1978 cloudburst dropped 30 cm of rain in 12 hours and broke its bunds, and Cyclone Thane made landfall nearby in 2011. Size earthworks, roofs and tree cover for extreme monsoon and cyclone events.

factsLong.founded: 28 February 1968 (inauguration), by Mirra Alfassa ('The Mother') under the Sri Aurobindo Society, with UNESCO endorsement
factsLong.residents: 3,527 (Auroville census 2026: 2,865 adults, 662 children); 3,296 in an early-2025 count
factsLong.nations: 60 nationalities (census 2026); India 1,888, France 413, Germany 233, Italy 161, USA 103
factsLong.area: About 20 sq km master-plan area: a city of 2.5 km diameter plus a Green Belt (5 km overall diameter), mostly in Tamil Nadu's Villupuram district, with a small part in Puducherry
factsLong.landOwned: About half of the master-plan land (Auroville says ~10% of the City Area and ~65% of the Green Belt are still to be bought); the Foundation said it owned about 850 ha in 2022
